accident_report:
Vehicle initialization
On a straight, downhill, one-way roadway with three lanes and a wide right shoulder, under nighttime conditions with a wet road surface, three vehicles are traveling in the same direction. V1 is in lane 2, positioned ahead of the others, traveling at 70 km/h with a steady cruising state and intending to maintain lane and speed. V2 is directly behind V1 in lane 2 at a close following distance of approximately 10 meters, traveling at 90 km/h and intending to continue following without changing lanes. V3 is in lane 1 (rightmost lane), slightly behind V2 by about 5 meters, traveling at 60 km/h and maintaining a steady speed, intending to continue forward without lane change.

Scenario development
As the vehicles proceed downhill, the gravitational effect causes all vehicles to experience a natural acceleration tendency. V1, approaching a section where the wet road reduces tire-road friction, detects a minor disturbance ahead (e.g., reduced traction zone) and applies moderate braking, reducing speed from 70 km/h to 50 km/h. Due to the wet surface and downhill gradient, V1’s deceleration is slightly less efficient than expected.

V2, following too closely and traveling at 90 km/h, encounters a large speed differential with V1. The driver of V2 perceives the deceleration of V1 with a slight delay due to nighttime visibility limitations. When V2 initiates braking, it applies emergency braking, attempting to reduce speed rapidly. However, because of the wet and downhill conditions, the available friction is insufficient, leading to extended braking distance and partial loss of tire grip.

At the same time, V3 in lane 1 observes V2’s abrupt deceleration and attempts to respond by braking from 60 km/h to 40 km/h. The wide shoulder to the right gives V3 an option to evade, but due to the wet surface, V3 avoids steering sharply and maintains lane while decelerating.

As V2 continues emergency braking, the insufficient friction and large initial speed difference prevent it from matching V1’s reduced speed in time. V2 begins to slightly drift forward despite braking effort. V1, still decelerating on the slippery downhill, cannot accelerate away to create more gap.

Result
The first collision occurs when V2 rear-ends V1 in lane 2 at an impact speed of approximately 40 km/h relative speed. The collision is directly caused by the combined effects of close following distance, large speed difference, emergency braking under wet and downhill conditions, and reduced nighttime visibility.
